name: Lucerne
model: written by hand (Claude) from the Urdu KB

aspects.overview: Lucerne (alfalfa) is a legume fodder rich in protein, vitamins, calcium and phosphorus. One sowing gives green fodder all year round for several years (6 to 7 years), and as a legume it fixes nitrogen from the air and improves the soil. It is hardier than berseem and oats: it tolerates severe cold, frost and strong heat. Semi-arid areas suit it best; irrigated lucerne does very well in dry areas, while humid weather doesn't suit it. Best soil: fertile, well-drained loam rich in calcium; waterlogged and saline soils are not suitable. Yield: about 1,000 maunds of green fodder per acre per year, and 2 to 3 maunds of seed per acre in good weather.
aspects.varieties:
Approved varieties (Fodder Research Institute Sargodha): Sarsabz, Naimat and Sargodha Lucerne 2002. Naimat also suits saline (kallar) land. Punjab Lucerne is less affected by stem rot.
Seed rate: 4 to 6 kg per acre by drill or line sowing (kera), 6 to 8 kg per acre broadcast.
Seed quality: use pure, clean, healthy seed; good seed is yellow, poor seed is reddish-brown. Market seed often contains shaftal, chicory (kasni), riwari and onion-weed seed; if chicory is mixed in, soak in a 5 percent salt solution, remove the floating seed and wash well. Inoculate the seed with bacteria (rhizobium) as for berseem. Seed is available from the Punjab Seed Corporation and the fodder research institutes at Sargodha, Bahawalpur and Faisalabad.
aspects.sowing:
Best time: 15 October to 15 November; earlier sowing gives more fodder. For a seed crop, sowing can go on until February.
Land: since the crop lasts 6 to 7 years, prepare the land well: one turn of a soil-turning plough, then 4 to 5 ploughings with planking until soft and fine; level with a laser land leveller.
Sowing: in well-prepared soil at workable moisture (wattar), in lines with a single-row drill or seed drill. Seed must not go deeper than 1.5 inches or germination suffers. Lines 1 foot apart for fodder, 1.5 feet for seed.
aspects.fertilizer: Get a soil test to fix the right amounts; for average soil: needs 23 kg nitrogen, 35 kg phosphorus and 12 kg potash per acre. Apply 1.5 bags DAP, half a bag of urea and half a bag of SOP; or 2 bags Nitrophos, 1.5 bags SSP and half a bag of SOP; or 4 bags SSP (18 percent), 1 bag urea and half a bag of SOP. Nitrogen can be given after each cut as the crop needs. Because the crop lasts years, re-apply phosphorus and potash over time. If stem rot appears, reduce nitrogen.
aspects.irrigation: First irrigation three weeks after sowing, then as needed. Lucerne's roots go very deep, so it tolerates water shortage well: usually one irrigation per cut, two in drier areas. In summer water every 15 to 20 days. Reduce water in February (black spot). In the seed crop, water as needed during flowering and pollination; after the seed harvest, irrigation restarts growth. Don't over-water.
aspects.pests_diseases:
Diseases:
Stem rot (fungus): white cottony growth on the lower stems; plants rot and wilt, in patches, usually January–February. Control: deep ploughing, level land, lower seed rate, no over-watering, keep water from diseased fields away from healthy ones, rotate crops, use potash and not too much nitrogen, don't grow host crops nearby. Chemical: after cutting, spray difenoconazole 1.5 ml per litre of water or sulphur 2 g per litre.
Stem/collar canker (fungus): sunken spots on the lower stem, which rots and turns black, then plants dry. Keep fields level so water doesn't stand, don't over-water, don't grow lucerne on that field for 3 to 4 years. Chemical: after cutting, spray cymoxanil + mancozeb 2 g per litre or chlorothalonil + metalaxyl-M 2 cc per litre.
Black spot (fungus): dark brown oval spots on leaves and stems; stems rot in severe attack. Water less in February; after cutting spray difenoconazole 1 cc per litre or sulphur 2 g per litre.
Root rot (wilt): plants wilt suddenly, pull out easily, root bark rotten. Treat seed with a recommended fungicide, cut early, don't water without need, don't mix lucerne with oats where the disease is expected, rotate, use a lower seed rate, and don't grow lucerne for 3 to 4 years where the disease occurred.
Rule: never spray the crop meant for fodder. Spray only seed crops, or spray after cutting the fodder, in the morning or evening to protect bees. Nothing should be sprayed 20 to 25 days before cutting.
Armyworm (lashkari sundi): greenish-brown caterpillar with yellow stripes and two black spots behind the head; curls up when touched. From February–March it eats leaves down to the veins, plus flowers and buds. Don't spray full-grown caterpillars; wait until they pupate. Keep the crop weed-free, use light and sex-pheromone traps, and dig water-filled trenches with kerosene around badly hit fields so caterpillars can't move on. In severe attack, after cutting, spray per acre 50 ml flubendiamide, or 40 to 50 ml chlorantraniliprole, or 200 ml lufenuron.
American bollworm: eats leaves; hay crops suffer most. If essential, cut the fodder and then spray per acre 40 ml spinosad, or 25 ml flubendiamide, or 40 to 50 ml chlorantraniliprole, or 200 ml emamectin benzoate, or 200 ml lufenuron. Use light and pheromone traps; check seed crops and spray while caterpillars are young.
Looper (kubri sundi): green caterpillar that loops when moving; webs and eats tender leaves. Same rules: don't spray fodder, spray after cutting; trenches with kerosene around fields.
Whitefly (seed crop): sucks sap, leaves turn yellow with black sooty mould. Spray per acre 250 ml acetamiprid, or 400 ml flonicamid, or 500 ml pyriproxyfen.
Thrips (seed crop): suck sap so leaves dry. Spray 200 ml chlorfenapyr per acre, and use yellow or blue sticky traps.
Aphid (sust tela): dark green, sucks sap, sooty mould follows. Sow treated seed; never spray the fodder crop. On the seed crop spray per acre 200 ml imidacloprid or nitenpyram, or 250 ml acetamiprid or bifenthrin.
Shoot fly: enters and dries the shoots; in severe attack cut the fodder, then spray 200 ml imidacloprid or emamectin benzoate per acre.
Fodder weevil: larva and adult eat green leaf tissue and new shoots; cut the fodder early. On the seed crop spray 40 to 50 ml flubendiamide or chlorantraniliprole per acre.
Lygus and sting bugs: damage buds, flowers and green pods so flowers drop and seed shrivels, mostly in the seed crop. Spray a recommended insecticide.
aspects.weeds:
Frequent cutting helps control weeds; rotate with other rabi crops.
Itsit: spray pendimethalin 1.5 litres per acre three weeks to a month before sowing and irrigate; plough at wattar and leave open.
Ghabbal grass: spray quizalofop 350 to 400 ml per acre.
Do not hoe right after spraying: dust can carry the chemical into the farmer's body.
aspects.harvesting:
Fodder: lucerne gives cuts all year; for hay cut at about 10 percent flowering. No spray of any kind 20 to 25 days before cutting.
Seed: stop cutting for fodder by the end of March. Beehives near large seed fields improve pollination and seed yield. Harvest the seed crop only when fully ripe, never green, timed so ripe pods don't drop in the field. On large areas use a combine harvester; otherwise cut, tie bundles, leave them to dry in the field and thresh with a thresher. Clean seed with an iron sieve and store in cloth or jute bags in a dry, airy store.
aspects.machinery: Laser land leveller for levelling; single-row drill or seed drill for sowing; combine harvester or thresher for the seed crop.
aspects.other: One sowing lasts 6 to 7 years, so land preparation is worth extra care.

timing.sowing: 15 October to 15 November (seed crop up to February)
timing.harvesting: fodder cuts all year; seed crop when fully ripe after fodder cutting stops at end of March
